# **Executive Summary**

 

GoHighLevel is an all-in-one marketing platform — CRM, email marketing, SMS, funnels, websites, calendars, automations, reputation management, invoicing, and more — sold to agencies and businesses at $97 to $497 per month. It also has a white-label mode: for $300 to $500 per month flat (a fixed fee that never scales with customer count), any agency can rebrand GoHighLevel as their own software, set their own price, and sell it to whatever audience they want. Most are doing significantly more. All of them built on top of software they did not write, do not maintain, and pay a flat $300 to $500 per month for regardless of how many customers they have.

# **PART 01 — What Is White-Label SaaS? The GoHighLevel Model Explained**

 

## **The Core Concept**

White labeling means putting your own brand on someone else's product and selling it to your audience. In physical goods, it is how store-brand products work — the same factory makes the generic and the name-brand versions, and the retailer slaps their logo on the generic and sells it at a markup. In software, the same principle applies but with dramatically better economics: the underlying software costs a fixed monthly fee regardless of how many customers you acquire on top of it.

 

GoHighLevel (also called GHL or High Level) is the underlying platform for every business in this episode. It provides: CRM, email marketing, SMS marketing, funnel builder, website builder, calendar booking, automation workflows, reputation management tools, invoicing, courses, memberships, and community features. As a white-label platform, it allows agencies and entrepreneurs to rebrand all of this as their own software, set their own pricing, and sell it to whichever niche they choose. GoHighLevel gets paid $300 to $500 per month. The white-labeler keeps everything else.

 

## **The Financial Structure**

| Who | What They Pay/Receive | Fixed or Variable | What They Do |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| GoHighLevel | Receives $300–$500/month from white-labeler (regardless of how many customers white-labeler has) | Fixed for GoHighLevel | Builds and maintains the underlying software, servers, security, and new features |
| White-label business (you) | Pays $300–$500/month to GoHighLevel; receives whatever you charge customers | Fixed cost; variable revenue | Brands, sells, and supports the software in a specific niche; sets own pricing |
| End customer (notary, gym, tutor) | Pays $97–$600/month to white-label business | Variable; set by white-labeler | Uses the software for their business; typically has no idea GoHighLevel is underneath |

 

## **The Math That Makes This Powerful**

GoHighLevel charges you $300 to $500 per month no matter how many customers you have. If you have 10 customers paying $97/month, your revenue is $970 and your GoHighLevel bill is $300. Net margin before support and ads: $670. If you have 1,000 customers paying $97/month, your revenue is $97,000 and your GoHighLevel bill is still $300. Net margin before support and ads: $96,700. The same fixed cost produces wildly different margins depending on your customer count. Every new customer you acquire after your first handful is almost pure profit from a software infrastructure perspective.

 

| Customers | Monthly Revenue (at $97/month avg) | GoHighLevel Cost | Gross Margin Before Support/Ads | Implied Gross Margin % |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 10 | $970 | $300–$500 | $470–$670 | 48–69% |
| 100 | $9,700 | $300–$500 | $9,200–$9,400 | 95–97% |
| 500 | $48,500 | $300–$500 | $48,000–$48,200 | 99% |
| 1,000 (Diamond Award minimum) | $97,000 | $300–$500 | $96,500–$96,700 | 99%+ |
| 1,000 (at $200/month average, like Push Press) | $200,000 | $300–$500 | $199,500–$199,700 | 99%+ |

 

# **PART 02 — The GoHighLevel Diamond Award: How to Spot $100K+ Monthly Businesses**

 

## **What the Diamond Award Proves**

GoHighLevel publicly awards SaaS companies built on its platform based on the number of monthly recurring revenue customers they maintain. The Diamond Award is the highest public tier and requires a minimum of 1,000 paying monthly recurring customers. This is not a self-reported number. GoHighLevel verifies and certifies it. Every company in this episode has been verified as having at least 1,000 customers.

 

The financial implication: 1,000 customers at even the lowest pricing seen in this episode ($97/month for notary software) equals $97,000 per month in revenue. This is the minimum. Companies charging $200/month average (like Push Press) hit $200,000/month at the same customer count. Companies charging $500/month (like Zappy Chat's unlimited tier) hit $500,000/month. Diamond Award \= confirmed $100K+/month minimum, with most well above that number.

 

## **How to Find Diamond Award Winners**

GoHighLevel maintains a public leaderboard of award winners. The host used this list as his research source — 'I just spent the weekend digging through this list right here. These are private companies. You and I usually have no idea what private companies make, but every business on this list has over 1,000 paying customers.' The list is publicly accessible. Any entrepreneur researching niches to enter can browse the Diamond Award winners, see which niches are already proven, and study those businesses before deciding which to emulate.

# **PART 03 — Business 7: Loan Signing System (Notary Software) — Mark Wills**

 

## **What the Business Is**

Loan Signing System was built by Mark Wills, a notary trainer who had spent years training mobile notaries on how to build their businesses. He knew the notary industry deeply — the pain points, the workflows, the things notaries were Googling at 11 PM. He took GoHighLevel, branded it as software specifically for mobile notaries, and launched it at $97/month or $1,000/year. The software gives notaries a CRM to track clients and appointments, manage their emails and communications, and organize their business operations.

 

## **The Pattern It Establishes**

Mark Wills started as a notary trainer, not a software developer. He built trust in the notary community by selling a course for approximately $400 — teaching people how to build a notary business. Once notaries trusted him and had built their businesses, he offered them software to manage what they had built. The course created the audience; the software monetized the audience on a recurring basis. His GoHighLevel bill: $300–$500/month forever. His revenue: minimum $97,000/month (1,000 customers at $97 each), almost certainly much higher given that this is the maximum award tier.

 

*Mark Wills's business on the Wayback Machine: launched approximately 2024 (about 2 years before the episode). The website design was described by the host as 'not great' — and the host was being generous. His conclusion: 'This should give you hope and inspiration. Oftentimes the best looking websites don't convert that well anyway.' A functional, ugly website that solves a real problem for a specific niche beats a beautiful website for a vague audience every time.*

 

| Element | Mark Wills's Approach | What You Can Copy |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Background | Notary trainer; spent years in the notary community | Find an industry you have worked in, studied, or trained others in |
| Trust-building phase | Sold a $400 course teaching notaries how to build their business | Build an audience through education first; course, YouTube channel, newsletter, coaching |
| Software product | GoHighLevel white-labeled as notary CRM | Find the CRM / workflow pain point in your niche; white-label GoHighLevel as the solution |
| Pricing | $97/month or $1,000/year | Monthly recurring is the correct model; $97 is the floor GoHighLevel recommends for profitability |
| Marketing | Notary community already trusted him from course business | You already have an audience from the service/training phase; convert them to software customers |
| Website quality | 'Not great' — host's polite description | Do not let imperfect design stop you from launching; shipping beats perfecting |
| Verification | GoHighLevel Diamond Award: 1,000+ customers | Set Diamond Award as your 2–3 year target; it means $100K+/month minimum |

 

# **PART 04 — Business 6: Push Press (Gym Management Software)**

 

## **What the Business Is**

Push Press is gym management software. It charges $229 per month with a $700 setup fee on its entry-level plan, with higher plans ranging up to $550 to $600 per month. The host used a conservative average of $200/month across all customers to estimate revenue at Diamond Award level: minimum $200,000/month, with setup fees, upsells, and other revenue lines likely pushing the total well above $5 million per year.

 

## **The Genius of the Wedge Strategy**

Push Press did not start as a full gym management CRM. It started as check-in software — just one feature: a digital check-in system for gym members. That is it. No CRM. No email marketing. No billing. Just: members scan in when they arrive. This hyper-specialized entry point had two advantages. First, it solved a concrete, immediate problem that every gym owner had. Second, it was so specific that it was non-threatening — it was not asking the gym owner to change their entire business management system, just to add one small tool. Push Press's core product has processed over one million check-ins, establishing the trust and usage data that justified expanding into a full CRM.

 

The host's strategic framing: 'Unbundle one little feature from a bigger piece of software, sell that hard, and then start giving them upsells and more and more software offerings.' The check-in feature was the wedge. The CRM was the upsell that became the main product. Once gym owners had already integrated Push Press into their daily operations for check-ins, switching costs made them far more likely to expand into the CRM rather than switch to a competitor. The trust was established; the expansion was natural.

 

## **The G2 Wedge-Finding Method**

The host described a specific tactic for finding the wedge feature in any niche: go to g2.com (a software review platform), find the leading software in your target niche, collect all the user reviews, paste them into ChatGPT, and ask 'What features do users say are missing?' The answer is your wedge. Build that missing feature as a GoHighLevel snapshot. Pitch it as the solution to the most common complaint about the existing market leader. You are not competing with the whole product — you are solving one specific pain point better than anyone else does.

 

| Phase | What Push Press Did | General Playbook |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Phase 1: Wedge entry | Built check-in software only; solved one specific gym problem | Find the single most-complained-about missing feature in your niche via G2 reviews; build that |
| Phase 2: Trust building | 1 million+ check-ins processed; deeply embedded in gym operations | Get customers dependent on the wedge feature before introducing anything new |
| Phase 3: CRM upsell | Added full CRM as an upsell to existing check-in customers | Introduce the bigger product (GoHighLevel white-label) as a natural add-on to existing customers |
| Phase 4: Full platform | $229–$600/month plans; setup fees; growing MRR | Price on value; add setup fees; add premium tiers; the product suite sells itself to warm customers |

 

# **PART 05 — Business 5: Scale Tutor — The Tutor CRM from the UK**

 

## **What the Business Is**

Scale Tutor (formerly called Tutor Boss) was founded by Elliot Phillips in the UK. The business helps tutors and online educators find more customers and manage their lead generation through software. Their publicly claimed stats: 20,000 students enrolled, $10 million in income generated for tutors, 250,000 leads generated. They have helped over 1,000 educators — the GoHighLevel Diamond Award threshold. Elliot Phillips is not a tech person. He started working with online educators as a service provider, built trust in that community, and then built software for the audience he was already serving.

 

## **The Rebranding Insight**

The host noted the rebrand from Tutor Boss to Scale Tutor — same founder, same business, same GoHighLevel backend. The rebrand tells a story about how these businesses evolve: the original name reflected the founder's original framing (boss your tutoring business); the new name reflects the customer's aspiration (scale your tutoring business). The product did not change. The positioning did. The lesson: brand and positioning matter even when the underlying product is identical. A rebrand to better reflect customer goals can drive growth without changing anything about the software.

 

## **The Consistent Pattern**

The host identified Scale Tutor as following exactly the same playbook as Loan Signing System: 'They're starting as service businesses or training businesses in their niche. They're starting with what they know because they know the pain points. They built the painkiller. Remember, painkillers, not vitamins, have to haves, not nice to haves. That's what they're doing.' Elliot did not sit down one day and decide to build tutor software because he saw a market opportunity. He was already working with tutors and online educators. He knew their specific frustrations — too many tabs open, no good way to manage leads, no CRM built for their specific needs. He built the exact solution his existing clients needed and sold it to the community he was already trusted in.

 

| Business | Founder Background | Initial Niche Work | Software Built | Public Stats |

| Loan Signing System | Notary trainer and practitioner | Trained mobile notaries via $400 course | GoHighLevel CRM for mobile notaries; $97/month | Diamond Award (1,000+ customers); $100K+/month |
| Scale Tutor | Worked with online educators as service provider | Led generation and marketing services for tutors | GoHighLevel CRM for tutors and online educators | 20K students enrolled; $10M income generated; 250K leads; Diamond Award |
| Push Press | Not explicitly stated; clearly deep gym industry knowledge | Check-in software as the initial wedge product | GoHighLevel gym management CRM | 1M+ check-ins; Diamond Award; estimated $5M+/year |

 

# **PART 06 — Business 4: IUL Insiders — Life Insurance Tech Ecosystem**

 

## **What the Business Is**

IUL Insiders (IUL stands for Index Universal Life) targets insurance agents who sell complex life insurance products. This business does something more sophisticated than just white-labeling a CRM: it white-labels both the software and the insurance product itself. Insurance agents who use IUL Insiders pay for access to: a GoHighLevel-powered CRM (labeled as their software tools), a mastery training library, weekly coaching calls, and a community — all within the GoHighLevel platform. And the insurance product they are trained to sell is also a white-labeled resale, with agents making $20,000 to $100,000 per case.

 

## **The Pricing Structure**

The pricing tiers revealed in the episode: Ignite package at $500 for 90 days then $180/month. A middle package at $800/month ($400 for 12 months paid annually). A top-tier package that requires clicking an 'Apply Now' button — which the host noted is a signal that the top tier is expensive and requires qualification before being told the price. The GoHighLevel cost to IUL Insiders is still $300 to $500/month flat. The IUL Insiders' revenue from each customer: $180 to $800+/month recurring. The margin is extraordinary.

 

## **The Ecosystem Lock-In**

The host described the stickiness of the IUL Insiders model as the most sophisticated in the episode: 'Think of how sticky that is. You can't switch your CRM software when your entire commission pipeline lives inside of it. And that's what they're doing. They're selling a whole ecosystem. When your training relationships are inside the software, your peer group, the community, it's all in there. So, they're not going to churn.'

 

Every element of an insurance agent's professional life that IUL Insiders hosts inside GoHighLevel becomes a switching cost. Their client records are in the CRM. Their training and credentials are in the mastery library. Their peer relationships are in the community. Their accountability is in the weekly coaching calls. Switching away from IUL Insiders does not just mean losing a software subscription — it means losing an entire professional support ecosystem. This is deliberate product design, not an accident. It is the most powerful churn prevention strategy of any business in this episode.

 

| IUL Insiders Component | Built On | Switching Cost It Creates |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Software tools (CRM, pipeline management) | GoHighLevel CRM | Client records, pipeline stages, commission tracking — all live here; switching means rebuilding from scratch |
| Mastery library (training content) | GoHighLevel courses and memberships | Certifications, completed training, reference materials — stored and searchable; leaving means losing access |
| Weekly coaching calls | GoHighLevel calendar and video integration | Ongoing accountability relationships with coaches; leaving means ending those relationships |
| Community and peer group | GoHighLevel community (GoCollab integration) | Professional relationships, deal-sharing, referral networks built inside the platform |
| Insurance product itself | White-labeled resale arrangement | If IUL Insiders provides access to specific insurance products, switching software might mean losing product access |

 

## **The Niche-Finding Method for This Playbook**

The host described how to find niches like IUL Insiders: 'Just go to YouTube and search any niche plus training, academy, certification. Anyone charging $10,000 plus and pulling in over 100 students should be running this play.' If there is already a training market of significant size in a niche, there is a software market waiting to be built for that same community. The training audience already understands they need to invest in their business. They are predisposed to paying for tools. You build the tools they need and sell to the community the trainer has already qualified.

 

# **PART 07 — Business 3: Zappy Chat — Path B: Selling to GoHighLevel Users**

 

## **What Makes This Different**

Every other business in this episode sells GoHighLevel (white-labeled) to end customers who may not know GoHighLevel exists. Zappy Chat does something different: it sells to GoHighLevel users themselves. Specifically, it sells AI chatbot snapshots — essentially plugin-style automation packages that other GoHighLevel agencies can install inside their own accounts to offer AI chatbot capabilities to their clients. Zappy Chat is not competing in a niche market; it is selling a tool to the 70,000+ GoHighLevel agencies that are already actively looking for ways to enhance their own products.

 

## **The Pricing**

Zappy Chat charges $200 per month per sub-account or $500 per month for unlimited sub-accounts. A GoHighLevel agency that pays $500/month for unlimited access can offer AI chatbot capabilities to all of its own clients under its own branding. At Diamond Award level (1,000+ customers), if they are all paying the unlimited tier, that is $500,000/month — $6 million per year. This is the highest potential revenue ceiling of any business in the episode.

 

## **Path A vs. Path B**

The host named these two approaches explicitly: Path A is white-labeling GoHighLevel for a specific niche (notaries, gyms, tutors, insurance agents). Path B is building tools or add-ons that GoHighLevel agencies buy to enhance their own products. Path B has a different competitive environment: instead of competing with other white-labelers in a specific niche, you are selling to the entire GoHighLevel ecosystem — 70,000+ agencies — all of whom are already sophisticated software users who understand the value of paid tools. Path B is harder to discover but easier to sell once found: your customers are business owners who buy software professionally, not end consumers who need to be educated about what a CRM is.

 

| Factor | Path A: Niche White-Label | Path B: GoHighLevel Add-On (Zappy Chat) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Target customer | End businesses in a specific niche (notaries, gyms, tutors) | GoHighLevel agencies and white-labelers (other businesses doing Path A) |
| Niche competition | Competitors: other white-labelers serving the same niche; some traditional SaaS players | Competitors: other GoHighLevel plugin/snapshot sellers; 229 apps in the GoHighLevel marketplace |
| Customer discovery | Find niche communities, influencers, Facebook groups, trade associations | Find GoHighLevel Facebook groups, Slack communities, the GoHighLevel marketplace itself |
| Pricing leverage | Limited by what niche customers will pay ($97–$600/month) | Higher ceiling because you are selling to business owners who understand software ROI ($200–$500/month) |
| Churn dynamics | Depends on how embedded the software is in the niche customer's workflow | Selling to agencies who have many clients — each lost agency client \= multiple lost end-customers |
| Revenue ceiling | 1,000 niche customers x $97 \= $97K/month | 1,000 agency customers x $500 \= $500K/month |
| Best for | Someone with niche expertise who knows specific industry pain points | Someone with GoHighLevel expertise who can identify missing features agencies need |

 

## **The GoHighLevel Marketplace**

The GoHighLevel app store — equivalent to an App Store but for GoHighLevel plugins and snapshots — has 229 apps at the time of the episode. The host's specific recommendation: 'Look for the gaps. What's missing? What's outdated? What could be 10 times better? What's trending right now? Build that. Sell it for $300 one time or $47 a month. Undercut them on price. 200 customers and you're making six figures a year.' Some apps in the marketplace have tens of thousands of installs — proof that the market for GoHighLevel add-ons is real, active, and paying.

## **You Do Not Need to Live There**

The host was explicit: 'You don't need to live in the country that you're launching a GHL clone in.' An American who speaks Spanish can launch a GoHighLevel clone for Colombia without ever visiting Colombia. The software is the same. The snapshot translates automatically. The support documentation is generated by AI in the target language. The marketing targets Facebook and Instagram audiences in the country. The payment processing (Stripe) handles international currencies. The only requirement is language access — and even that can be partially handled by AI translation with native-speaker review.

 

# **PART 09 — Business 1: ClickSlow — The Bankruptcy Case Study**

 

## **What They Did**

ClickSlow launched in late 2021 / early 2022 as a GoHighLevel white-label — websites, funnels, courses, memberships, CRM, payments, all the standard features — at $97 to $497 one-time pricing. Not per month. One time. They accumulated thousands of customers paying a single fee for what they described as lifetime access. The website looked clean and professional. The product worked. They reached significant customer counts and appeared to be succeeding.

 

## **Why They Went Bankrupt**

GoHighLevel charges $300 to $500 per month forever. ClickSlow was charging customers $97 once. The math: at $97 per customer and $300/month in platform costs, ClickSlow needed to acquire a new paying customer every three days just to cover its GoHighLevel bill. And that was only the platform cost — not customer support, not marketing, not any other operating cost. The host's analysis: 'After that, every customer was actively costing them money. It almost becomes like a pyramid scheme or a Ponzi scheme where you have to keep acquiring more customers just to keep paying your bills because there's nothing recurring.'

 

The Trustpilot evidence: ClickSlow has a 2.4-star rating. Reviews describe bad customer service and, more critically, a bait-and-switch: customers who thought they had paid for lifetime access were eventually asked to pay monthly when the company could no longer sustain the one-time pricing model. The host's verdict: 'How to win? Pick a name better than ClickSlow. Do what you say you're going to do.'

 

| Metric | ClickSlow (Failed) | Winning Model (Monthly Recurring) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Pricing structure | $97 one-time (claimed lifetime) | $97–$600/month recurring |
| GoHighLevel cost | $300–$500/month (fixed) | $300–$500/month (fixed) |
| Break-even customers | Must acquire new customers every 3 days just to cover GHL cost alone | At 4 customers paying $97/month, GHL cost is covered; everything after is profit |
| Month 8 economics (hypothetical) | Revenue from $97 customer used up; customer now costs net money every month | Month 8 customer still paying $97/month; revenue ongoing; still profitable |
| Churn consequence | Losing a customer saves money (one less support cost) | Losing a customer costs $97/month recurring; churn directly hurts P\&L |
| Acquisition machine requirement | Must constantly acquire new customers to pay ongoing bills; no choice | Can grow steadily; do not need to run at maximum speed just to maintain |
| Long-term outcome | Bankrupt; customers felt deceived; brand destroyed | All Diamond Award winners charging monthly; proven model |

 

*The host's critical checklist question: 'When you copy any one of these businesses, ask yourself: does my pricing cover my GoHighLevel bill plus my time plus my ads plus my support every single month forever? If the answer is no, you don't have a business. You've got a 24-month time bomb.'*

 

# **PART 10 — The Two Paths: White-Label Niche vs. GoHighLevel Add-On**

 

## **Choosing Between Path A and Path B**

The host summarized the two strategic choices available to anyone entering the GoHighLevel ecosystem. Both are valid. The choice depends on what skills, relationships, and knowledge you are starting with.

 

## **Path A: White-Label for a Specific Niche**

This is the Loan Signing System, Push Press, Scale Tutor, IUL Insiders, and Techmatics play. Pick a niche you know from experience, white-label GoHighLevel for that niche, and sell it as specialized software to businesses in that industry. Competition comes from other white-labelers in the same niche plus traditional SaaS. The customer is the end business owner who may not know GoHighLevel exists.

 

## **Path B: Build Tools for GoHighLevel Agencies**

This is the Zappy Chat play. You build features, snapshots, or add-ons that other GoHighLevel agencies buy to enhance their own products. The competitive landscape is the 229 apps in the GoHighLevel marketplace. The customer is a GoHighLevel agency — a sophisticated software buyer who understands ROI and will pay more for time-saving tools. The market is immediately accessible: GoHighLevel Facebook groups, Slack communities, and the GoHighLevel marketplace itself are where these customers already congregate.

 

| Question | Path A (Niche White-Label) | Path B (GoHighLevel Add-On) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Do you have niche industry expertise? | Required — industry knowledge is your competitive moat | Not required — GoHighLevel technical expertise is what matters |
| Do you know GoHighLevel deeply? | Basic knowledge sufficient; platform complexity is hidden from end customer | Required — you are selling to sophisticated GHL users who will test your product |
| Where do you find customers? | Industry Facebook groups, YouTube channels, trade associations, micro influencers in the niche | GoHighLevel Facebook groups, Slack communities, GoHighLevel marketplace |
| What is your pricing power? | Limited by what niche customers will accept ($97–$600/month) | Higher — agencies buy on ROI, not price sensitivity ($200–$500/month) |
| How competitive is it? | Depends entirely on chosen niche; many still wide open | 229 marketplace apps; but many are outdated or missing key features |
| What is the build effort? | Low — configure GoHighLevel snapshot for niche; add branding | Medium to high — need to actually build a functional add-on or snapshot product |
| Best entry point | You are already in an industry; you know the pain points | You have built with GoHighLevel extensively; you see what is missing |

 

# **PART 11 — The Pricing Imperative: Why Monthly Beats One-Time Forever**

 

## **The Lesson ClickSlow Taught With Bankruptcy**

The host's summary of the pricing lesson from this entire episode: 'The guys in this list of seven that I just covered, the ones that are really crushing it, are charging monthly. The notary guy, Push Press, the gym software, Scale Tutor, IUL Insider, Zappy Chat, Techmatics — they're all charging monthly. ClickSlow broke the pattern and they went bankrupt.' Six out of seven winners charge monthly. The seventh went bankrupt. The correlation is not subtle.

 

## **Why Monthly Recurring Revenue Is the Only Viable Model**

GoHighLevel's economics create an existential requirement for monthly revenue. The platform charges $300 to $500 per month regardless of your customer count. This is a fixed, recurring obligation that never goes away. If your revenue is not also recurring, you are on a treadmill: you must constantly acquire new paying customers just to maintain your current cost base, before you can even think about growth or profit. One bad month of acquisition and you are losing money on every existing customer.

 

Monthly recurring revenue solves this structurally: each new customer adds permanent monthly revenue to your base. A customer who signs up in January is still paying in December. Your GoHighLevel bill is covered from month two onward with a handful of customers, and every customer after that is incremental margin.

 

| Revenue Model | Month 1 Cash Flow | Month 6 Cash Flow | Month 12 Cash Flow | Sustainability | Used By |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| $97 one-time | $9,700 (100 new customers) | $0 from those 100; only new customers generate revenue | $0 from first 100; GHL cost still $300–$500/month | Requires constant acquisition to survive; ClickSlow's model | ClickSlow (bankrupt) |
| $97/month recurring | $9,700 (100 new customers) | $9,700 from same 100 \+ any new customers | $9,700 from same 100 \+ 11 months of additional acquisition | Fixed cost covered; every additional customer is profit | All 6 surviving businesses |
| $200/month recurring | $20,000 (100 customers) | $20,000+ from same 100 \+ growth | $20,000+ ongoing; potential $200K+ at 1,000 customers | Extraordinary margin structure | Push Press estimated average |
| $500/month recurring | $50,000 (100 customers) | $50,000+ ongoing; potential $500K+ at 1,000 customers | $6M annual run rate at Diamond Award level | Near-100% gross margin at scale | Zappy Chat (unlimited tier) |

 

## **Designing for Churn Resistance**

Monthly pricing is necessary but not sufficient. You also need to minimize churn — customers who cancel. The IUL Insiders model is the gold standard: every component of a customer's professional life (CRM, training, community, coaching) lives inside the platform. Canceling means losing all of it. For most white-label businesses, the equivalent is getting customers to use the platform for their client records, their email list, their calendar, and their automations — the more deeply embedded, the harder to leave.

 

# **PART 12 — Finding Your Niche: The Pattern Across All Seven Businesses**

 

## **The Universal Pattern**

Every successful business in this episode follows a version of the same origin story: the founder was already in an industry, developed genuine understanding of the pain points, built trust within that community, and then built software for the community they were already part of. None of them started by identifying a market opportunity from the outside and building cold. All of them started from the inside.

 

The host's framing: 'Everyone watching this right now has an unfair competitive advantage because you're in some industry. Whether you're an employee or an entrepreneur, doesn't matter.' If you have worked as a cashier, door dasher, plumber's assistant, dental receptionist, or gym front-desk worker — you know something about that industry that an outsider does not. That knowledge is your unfair advantage. The software is GoHighLevel. The niche knowledge is yours.

| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Mobile notaries | Scheduling chaos; no CRM for client tracking; no system for managing job pipeline | Calendar \+ CRM \+ automation workflows | Notaries who already run their own business; students of notary training courses |

| Dog groomers | Appointment scheduling; customer reminders; repeat booking tracking | Calendar \+ SMS automation \+ CRM | Independent groomers and small grooming businesses |
| Wedding photographers | Inquiry management; contract tracking; payment collection; album delivery | CRM \+ payments \+ client portal | Photographers who still use email and spreadsheets |
| Bail bondsmen | Client tracking; court date reminder automation; payment management | CRM \+ SMS automation \+ calendar | Independent bail bond agents in major metro markets |
| Estheticians / med spas | Appointment booking; client rebooking reminders; loyalty tracking | Calendar \+ SMS \+ CRM | Solo practitioners and small med spa chains |
| Roofers / home service contractors | Lead management; estimate follow-up; job status tracking | CRM \+ automation \+ invoicing | Independent contractors and small construction companies |
| Dentists | Appointment reminders; patient follow-up; review management | Calendar \+ SMS \+ reputation management | Independent dental practices not already on enterprise dental software |

 

## **The Boring Niche Principle**

The host's specific recommendation: 'The more boring the better, because it means more people are overlooking it. Boring industries have weaker competition, but they still have customers who are starving for help.' Bail bondsmen, dog groomers, and estheticians are not attractive industries to tech entrepreneurs. That is precisely why the competition for software in these niches is thin. The customers exist and they need tools. The only thing missing is someone who understands their specific workflow well enough to configure GoHighLevel appropriately and market it to them.

 

# **PART 13 — Customer Acquisition Without an Audience**

 

## **The Micro-Influencer Partnership Strategy**

The host introduced a specific customer acquisition approach for people who do not have an existing audience in the target niche: partner with micro-influencers who do. 'Micro-influencers with 5,000 to 50,000 followers and no idea how to build software — build this for them. Split it with them 50-50. Slide into their DMs on Twitter, Instagram, personal Facebook, Venmo, PayPal, anywhere that isn't crowded.'

 

A micro-influencer with 20,000 followers who teaches notaries how to build their business has exactly the audience the notary CRM needs. They have trust that would take you years to build. But they have not built the software. You have. The partnership offer: you build the white-labeled CRM, handle setup, and provide support. They promote it to their audience and handle the brand relationship. Revenue split 50/50. Both parties win.

 

## **The Venmo Cold Outreach Trick**

The host described a specific outreach hack that works because of how Venmo and PayPal handle unmapped email addresses: 'Send them a cent to their PayPal email and put in the message: Hey, I want to partner with you on something. Email me.' If the email address is not attached to a PayPal account, PayPal will repeatedly email the recipient about unclaimed money. PayPal wants them to create an account and claim the cent. Every follow-up email from PayPal includes the sender's message. It is spam-proof, compliant, and impossible to ignore because PayPal keeps sending it. The host's kicker: 'It's even better if they don't have a PayPal account at the email address you find for them.'

 

| Acquisition Channel | Best For | Cost | Notes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Micro-influencer partnership (50/50 split) | Anyone without an existing niche audience | Revenue share only — no upfront cost | Find influencers via YouTube, TikTok, Instagram in your target niche; propose partnership before building anything |
| Venmo/PayPal $0.01 outreach | Direct outreach to influencers or potential partners | Essentially $0 (fractions of a cent per send) | PayPal's spam-proof follow-up does the outreach work for you; unconventional enough to stand out |
| YouTube niche \+ 'training/academy/certification' search | Finding established training businesses to partner with | $0 | Identify people already teaching in your niche; propose adding software to their training offer |
| GoHighLevel Facebook groups | Path B (add-on) customer acquisition; also Path A peer networking | $0 (organic content) | 70,000+ agencies in these groups; announce your product; offer free trials |
| Meta ads (Facebook/Instagram) | Scaling once product is validated | $20–$100/day to start testing | Target by job title and industry; niche audiences are small enough to be cost-effective |
| G2 reviews mining | Finding what competitors' customers are complaining about | $0 | Paste reviews into ChatGPT; ask what features are missing; build those; market to reviewers who complained |
| Industry trade associations and conferences | In-person trust building; especially effective in old-school industries (notaries, bail bondsmen) | Variable; conference fees | Old-school industries respond better to in-person; digital marketing is less saturated there |

 

# **PART 14 — Six Reverse-Engineering Tools**

 

## **The Research Arsenal**

The host revealed six tools for reverse-engineering any business on the internet — in addition to 17 he shared in a prior episode. Used together, these tools allow you to understand any competitor's full marketing strategy, tech stack, customer acquisition methods, and team composition before deciding whether and how to enter their market.

 

| Tool | What It Does | Best Use Case | Cost |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| SpyFu (spyfu.com) | Shows every keyword a competitor has paid for in Google Ads over the past several years; maps their entire paid ad strategy | Understanding how an existing white-label SaaS is acquiring customers via Google; identifying ad spend and keyword focus | Paid subscription; various plans |
| Wappalyzer (Chrome extension) | Free Chrome extension; click any website and immediately see every piece of tech running on it — including if it is secretly GoHighLevel underneath the white-label branding | Confirming that a competitor is built on GoHighLevel; seeing what other tools they use (email platform, analytics, payments) | Free |
| publicwww.com | Searches the entire internet for specific code snippets — including Facebook pixel IDs; finds every website using a specific pixel ID | Discovering all websites owned by the same company or person; linking brands that share ad tracking infrastructure to find multi-brand operators | Paid; various plans |
| PredictLeads (predictleads.com) | Tracks hiring signals and product launch signals; alerts when a company suddenly hires multiple support or sales reps | Identifying when competitors are scaling; spotting fast-growing companies before they become widely known; timing market entry | Paid subscription |
| Apollo.io (apollo.io) | LinkedIn data with scraped email addresses for founders, executives, and professionals; enables direct outreach to specific company leadership | Finding and contacting founders of white-label SaaS businesses to study their background; reaching potential partnership targets | Freemium; paid tiers for larger volume |
| TheirStack.com (theirstack.com) | Tracks what technology stacks websites and apps use across millions of companies; can filter by niche and specific tool | Finding every business in a specific niche using a specific tool (e.g., every gym using a specific scheduling software); competitor research at scale | More affordable than BuiltWith; paid tiers |

 

## **Applying the Tools to the GoHighLevel Research Process**

The host described a specific research workflow: pick one of the seven businesses from the episode. Use the Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) to see what their website looked like at launch versus today. Read their G2 and Trustpilot reviews to understand customer pain points and praise. Look up their founder on Apollo.io to understand their background and whether they are building in public (which gives more intelligence). Use Wappalyzer to confirm whether the business is built on GoHighLevel. Use SpyFu to see their paid ad strategy. This complete picture of a competitor's full journey, tech stack, pricing evolution, and customer sentiment takes a few hours and gives you more strategic intelligence than most entrepreneurs gather in months of market research.

 

# **PART 15 — 30-Day Launch Plan**

 

## **Week 1: Research, Choose, and Validate**

**Day 1–2: Pick your business and study it**

Choose one of the seven businesses from the episode — whichever resonates most with your background and niche knowledge. Spend two days studying it: look up its Trustpilot and G2 reviews (take screenshots; paste into ChatGPT and ask what you can learn). Find its founder on LinkedIn and Apollo.io. Check the Wayback Machine at web.archive.org to see the website's evolution from launch to today. Use Wappalyzer to confirm the GoHighLevel foundation. Use SpyFu to see what keywords they buy. Build a complete picture of how this business was built, what customers love and hate, and where the gaps are.

 

**Day 3–4: Choose your niche**

Pick the niche you will serve. The host's criteria: ideally an industry you have worked in or know well, because you have unfair knowledge of their pain points. The more boring the niche, the better. If the industry does not have obvious tech-savvy competition, that is a signal — not a warning. Sign up for GoHighLevel using the link in the episode description for a 30-day free trial (14 days for standard signups; 30 days with the host's link). Do not pay for anything yet. Just poke around with all the features.

 

**Day 5–7: Validate before building**

Before configuring anything, validate that people in your niche will pay for software. The fastest validation: find five micro-influencers in your target niche on YouTube, Instagram, or TikTok. Reach out via DM or the Venmo/PayPal trick. Describe the software concept and propose a 50/50 partnership. If at least two respond with genuine interest, you have enough signal to proceed. Do not build anything until you have a distribution partner or a waitlist. The software takes 30 days to configure; the distribution is the hard part.

 

## **Week 2: Build the Core Product**

**Day 8–12: Configure your GoHighLevel snapshot**

A snapshot in GoHighLevel is a pre-configured template of all the settings, workflows, automations, and features you have built for your niche. This is what you are really selling — not the software itself, but the configuration of the software for a specific audience. Start with the most important features for your niche: for a notary CRM, that means a contact database, a job status pipeline, and an appointment calendar. Do not try to configure everything at once. Build the core features that solve the primary pain point. The wedge strategy from Push Press applies here: one great feature is better than 10 mediocre ones.

 

**Day 13–14: Set pricing and build the sales page**

Set your pricing at $97 to $297 per month — no one-time options, no lifetime deals. Make sure your pricing covers your GoHighLevel white-label cost ($300–$500/month) plus support time plus any ad spend, every month forever. Check with the host's checklist: 'Does my pricing cover my GoHighLevel bill plus my time plus my ads plus my support every single month forever?' If the answer is not yes at your expected customer count, raise the price. Build a simple sales page — even a Notion page or a GoHighLevel funnel — that describes the software, shows the pricing, and has a way for people to sign up. It does not need to look great. Mark Wills proved that.

 

## **Week 3: First Customers**

**Day 15–18: Launch to the influencer partner's audience**

If you secured a micro-influencer partner in Week 1, this is the moment they introduce the software to their audience. They post a video or email or story: 'I partnered with \[your brand\] to build software specifically for \[notaries/groomers/tutors/etc.\]. Here's a link to get started.' Your first customers should come in this week. Offer them direct onboarding support — get on calls, answer every question, iterate the product based on what confuses them. These first five to ten customers are the foundation of your case studies and the proof that the product works.

 

**Day 19–21: Get testimonials and case study data**

With your first customers onboarded and using the product, document everything. Ask them: what problem did this solve? How much time does it save you? What did you use before? Would you recommend it? Get them on a short video call if possible and record it. Even a text testimonial is valuable. These customer stories are the marketing material for every subsequent customer. You cannot generate fake social proof at the level of Mark Wills's notary community knowing and trusting him — but you can generate real social proof from real early customers.

 

## **Week 4: Build the Machine**

**Day 22–28: Systematize and scale**

By Week 4, you should have: a working GoHighLevel snapshot, two to ten paying customers, real testimonials, and a clear sense of what customers love and what needs improving. Now build the acquisition machine. If the influencer partner channel is working, bring on a second influencer in the same niche. If you are doing this without a partner, run your first $100 in Facebook ads targeted by job title (mobile notary, personal trainer, etc.) to your sales page. Iterate the ad creative based on results. The goal: make customer acquisition systematic and repeatable before the trial period ends.

 

**Day 29–30: Commit to monthly and set the Diamond Award target**

At the end of Month 1, you should know: whether the product resonates (people bought and stayed), whether the niche is accessible (you found influencer partners or customers through ads), and whether the unit economics work (pricing covers costs with margin). If yes to all three, commit to a 12-month run with the same niche and the same product. Set the Diamond Award (1,000 customers) as your 2–3 year target. At $97/month average, 1,000 customers is $97,000/month — $1.16M per year. From a $300–$500/month fixed cost. In a boring niche that nobody else is paying attention to.

 

# **Closing: Pick a Niche. Partner With a Creator. Copy Paste.**

 

 

A guy named Mark Wills trained notaries. He knew what notaries needed. He built a GoHighLevel CRM, put his own branding on it, and charged $97/month. He now has over 1,000 paying customers — the GoHighLevel Diamond Award, publicly verified. At minimum, $97,000/month. Probably more. His GoHighLevel bill: $300 to $500/month regardless. Website quality: 'not great' — the host's description. Time in business: approximately two years.

 

A woman in Australia built Techmatics — GoHighLevel for Australians. She did not need to be a tech founder. She did not need venture capital. She did not need a 100,000-follower audience. She needed to be in Australia, know that Australian small businesses needed marketing software, and know how to configure GoHighLevel. She has over 1,000 paying customers in a country with 26 million people. Between $2 million and $4 million per year by the host's estimate.

 

Zappy Chat sells AI chatbot plugins to the 70,000+ agencies already using GoHighLevel. $500/month per agency. Over 1,000 agencies paying. That is $500,000/month if they are all on the unlimited tier. Six million dollars per year. Selling to businesses who already understand software ROI. In a marketplace that already has their target customers.

 

The pattern is the same in all seven businesses: boring niche, software somebody else maintains, fixed cost that never scales, monthly recurring revenue, and deep knowledge of a specific audience's specific pain. The host's summary: 'Don't try to reinvent the wheel and be all innovative and disruptive. Just stick with what works because it's proven. Someone has gone before you. Remember, you don't want to be a pioneer. The pioneers are the ones that get shot with arrows.'

 

ClickSlow was the pioneer with one-time pricing. They went bankrupt. Six other companies with monthly pricing are each doing $100K to $500K per month. The experiment has been run. The lesson is documented. The only thing left is picking a niche and starting.

 

Estheticians. Bail bondsmen. Dog groomers. Wedding photographers. Tutors. Notaries. The more boring you think it sounds, the more likely nobody else is building it. And that boring niche has 10,000 businesses in it who are desperately using spreadsheets and Gmail and sticky notes to run their operations — and would pay $97/month to have something that works.

 

Pick the one that resonates. Spend a week studying the company from the episode that matches it most. Sign up for GoHighLevel with the 30-day trial. Find a micro-influencer in the niche and send them a cent on Venmo with a partnership proposal. Build the snapshot. Charge monthly. Cover your GoHighLevel bill. Keep your commitments. Do not be ClickSlow.
